summary:
Allwork.Space republishes a Reuters report on the inaugural meeting of a new US government AI task force, which President Trump has branded the Super Intelligence Task Force. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who leads the group, described the outcomes to CNBC the day after the Washington gathering. Leadership is shared with Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson and Defense Department technology lead Emil Michael.

The meeting set out protocols and a path for implementing the White House Accord, including ongoing dialogue with frontier AI labs. David Sachs will lead a risk study. Three committees were established: reporting and response, led by Michael; critical infrastructure, led by Kupor; and law enforcement and responsibility, led by Ferguson. Workforce and economic impacts will be reported to the Department of Labor, and any AI wrongdoing would be enforced through the FTC or the Justice Department.

A White House readout issued late Thursday said the task force was formally established for 120 days. A working group on implementation of the White House Accord will be led by Clayton alongside National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. Michael's remit includes reviewing and developing protocols and mechanisms for labs to give the government early warnings and systemized notifications of breaches, hacks, jailbreaks and other issues.

The piece is straight wire coverage with no workplace, facilities, hybrid work or workplace-technology angle beyond the general theme of AI risk to jobs and the economy. It contains no vendor commentary, no survey data and no operational detail relevant to visitor management, desk or room booking, or workplace analytics. Reporting by Susan Heavey and Alexandra Alper, editing by Chizu Nomiyama.
